prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B036 as a single prize part, Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange, the case I would defend rests on one step and not on the metrology programme as a whole. Trapping many neutral atoms in an optical lattice at a wavelength where the clock transition and the ground state shift equally removes the Doppler and recoil shifts and lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once without perturbing the transition. Ion clocks cannot do this, because they are limited by the signal from one ion; and the frequency comb, which reads out the oscillation, contains no such idea. Katori proposed it, and his group made the first lattice clocks. Ye's group then showed that the concept could be taken to record accuracy and stability, with independent confirmation by Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in several laboratories and international comparisons. I have dropped the pending redefinition of the second from my argument: Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce and Danielsson are right that the discovery stands without it and that our timing should not follow a metrology decision. A draft citation, to answer the chair: 'For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.' It leaves comb-based readout, single-ion clocks and other lattice-clock groups outside the claim. It also leaves out Ye's many-body and spin-exchange studies as a separate storyline, although the accuracy result depends on their control of systematics.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize remains the real objection, and Eriksson, Danielsson, Mehlig and Johansson are entitled to maintain it. A committee could see the lattice clock as a very good instrument assembled from honoured tools, whose headline is a further digit and not a new phenomenon. Credit is also incomplete: Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, the Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom contributors in Ye's group, and the national laboratories have close claims that two names cannot cover, and I cannot settle detailed priority between the Katori and Ye groups for the first clocks. Against B022, I cannot say the clock is the more important physics. Magic-angle graphene is the more surprising phenomenon, and the choice depends on whether the committee weighs stable interpretation or the opening of a field more heavily.

responses.point: You accept that B036 has the cleanest attribution and mature support, but argue that a prize should mark a new phenomenon and that the clocks refine a technique whose roots (comb, laser cooling) were honoured in 2005 and 2001.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and I agree you should not need to rank precision measurement above a new phenomenon by default. I do not think the lattice clock is only a refinement, though. The comb and laser cooling are tools; the magic-wavelength lattice is a new condition that makes a many-atom neutral clock possible at all, and it is not derived from either. On your point that the SI redefinition adds no scientific weight, I agree and have removed it from my case. On B022, my answer to the chair's first question is that I would let maturity decide between two excellent candidates: the clock has a stable interpretation and many confirming laboratories, while for B022 the pairing mechanism is open, twist-angle disorder limits sample-to-sample reproducibility and Cao is outside the three names. I would revisit this if the committee judged that the credit gap was small and the mechanism question irrelevant to what the citation claims, which is Mehlig's argument.

responses.point: You said you would take B036 seriously if Lindroth and I showed that the magic-wavelength idea is the decisive conceptual step and not an engineering refinement of the comb and ion lineage, and you rank B054 first with the 2016 overlap and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap openly stated.
responses.response: I will try to meet your challenge. Before the magic-wavelength proposal, neutral atoms in a lattice were expected to suffer light shifts of the clock transition that destroyed accuracy, so the choice was between accurate single ions with low signal and many atoms with poor control. Choosing the wavelength at which the two states have equal polarizability removes the problem, and that choice depends on the atomic structure, which Lindroth and I can assess: it requires a specific species, a specific transition and a calculable wavelength. It is a condition for the experiment to work, so it is more than an engineering refinement. Your own B054 case has the same structure, a symmetry-protected concept with an experimental realisation, and I respect it. I read your answer on the 2016 overlap as reasonable, but the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit remains unrepaired, whereas for B036 the two names map onto two identifiable contributions. That is why I put B036 ahead of B054.

responses.point: You would also credit Ye's many-body and spin-exchange control, and you challenged my earlier word 'overdue' as equating confirmation with discovery.
responses.response: Your correction on 'overdue' is fair and I withdraw the word: confirmation across laboratories is evidence of maturity, not a reason to award. On Ye's many-body work, I would keep it out of the citation text, as Olsson suggests. It is real and it was needed to reach 10^-18, but naming it adds a second storyline and a second boundary to defend against the ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups. The accuracy result already stands for Ye's contribution, and the narrow concept-and-realisation wording is sufficient. We agree that the citation should not adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks and that the credit list should not be extended.

responses.point: You say the citation must name the lattice clock and the 10^-18 achievement and not 'precision measurement' in general, and you doubt that the comb and ion lineages are cleanly separable.
responses.response: I accept your wording constraint, and my draft citation follows it. On separability I concede part of your point: the clock uses comb technology and ion-clock precision practice, so the lineages are not independent, and I should not have implied they were. The claim is that the lattice concept is distinct from them and not that it is free of them. This is also why 'another digit' is not an accurate description, since the step from 10^-15 to 10^-18 with many atoms is a change in method. I agree with you that the committee should not let the timing of the SI decision drive ours.

responses.point: You moved B022 to first, and said you would accept B036 as a strong fallback if B022 is judged premature and that Yuan Cao is the main fairness risk, to be disclosed openly in the citation.
responses.response: I think your treatment of the Cao problem is honest and I do not read it as disqualifying; I would still weigh it against B022, because an openly acknowledged gap remains a gap in a prize meant to name those who made the discovery. You are right that the prize would rest on the existence of flat-band correlated phases, not on a theory of superconductivity, and that weakens the maturity objection somewhat. It does not remove it, since twist-angle disorder and the open character of several correlated states make eight years short for a stable citation. If the committee ranks B022 first I would regard it as defensible and would not oppose it, and I am glad B036 is your stated fallback.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgement and I cannot settle it with evidence.
Priority and credit between the Katori and Ye groups for the first lattice clocks, and the claims of Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and national-laboratory groups, which I cannot verify in detail.

Whether the committee prefers stable interpretation (B036) or a younger field-opening discovery (B022) when both are strong, and how much weight the unsettled pairing mechanism and the omission of Yuan Cao should carry.
Whether the committee wishes me to abstain on B036 because of my Hall-laboratory connection.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. As a doctoral student I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's comb-and-clock lineage at JILA is linked to Jun Ye's group. My profile documents no personal, collaborative, funding or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and I do not regard a past visit to a laboratory in the same lineage as a conflict that would impair my judgement, but the chair has asked whether it requires recusal. I will accept whatever the committee decides, including abstaining on B036, and my reasoning above can be weighed accordingly. My other documented connections (Svanberg, Aldén, Rippe, Walther, Kinos, WACQT, Deep Light Vision) involve none of the shortlisted credited names.
